g.title: ciaddr=0, chaddr = the client's hardware address; the client waits 1-10s before the first send to desynchronize startup (§4.4.1)
lease=3600s, T1=1800s, T2=3150s; the server SHOULD check the address is not already in use, e.g. by an ICMP Echo Request (§3.1 item 2)
server A reads this as a declined offer and may return 192.0.2.10 to the pool (§3.1 item 4)
requested-ip=192.0.2.44, and the same 'secs' value and broadcast address as the DHCPDISCOVER, so every relay agent forwards it to the same servers (§3.1 item 3)
the server commits the binding to persistent storage; 'yiaddr' carries the selected address and the lease options carry T1 and T2 (§3.1 item 4)
the client broadcasts with sender-ip 0.0.0.0; a reply means the address is already in use (§4.4.1)
the client waits at least ten seconds before restarting (§3.1 item 5)
the selected server cannot satisfy the request; Figure 5 sends REQUESTING back to INIT on DHCPNAK (§4.4.5)
server B is unreachable; no DHCPACK arrives, which is what makes T2 fire (§4.4.5)
broadcast so that ANY server may extend the lease; this is why server A, which was not selected in §3.1, can answer it
the binding server is now A (§4.4.5)
Figure 3 captions the server side 'Discards lease'

g.text: DHCPREQUEST ciaddr=192.0.2.44 — unicast at T1, 0.5 x the lease (1800s)
DHCPREQUEST ciaddr=192.0.2.44 — unicast at T1, 0.5 x the lease (1800s)
Broadcast to 255.255.255.255 — ONE datagram that every DHCP server on the subnet receives; drawn once per recipient because FigDown has no fan-out (RFC 2131 §4.1)
Server's unsolicited offer of configuration parameters; the server need not reserve the address it offers (RFC 2131 §3.1 item 2)
Server commits the binding to persistent storage and confirms it (RFC 2131 §3.1 item 4)
Refusal or conflict — the client's notion of its address is wrong, or the address is already in use (RFC 2131 §3.1 items 4-5)
Addressed to one server only, using the address the client already holds (RFC 2131 §4.4.4)
The client's own check on the link before it trusts the address (RFC 2131 §4.4.1)

svg.metadata:
# FigDown — figures as text. Spec: https://github.com/FigDown/figdown
figdown 0.4 sequence title "DHCP lease acquisition, renewal and release (RFC 2131 §3.1, §4.4)"
# ── What this figure is ───────────────────────────────────────────── # The whole life of one DHCP lease, from a client with no address to # the DHCPRELEASE that gives it back: the four-message acquisition of # RFC 2131 §3.1 (drawn as Figure 3, "Timeline diagram of messages # exchanged between DHCP client and servers when allocating a new # network address"), the address check of §4.4.1, and the T1/T2 # reacquisition cycle of §4.4.5. The per-client state names are the # ones RFC 2131 §4.4 Figure 5 uses. # # THIS IS THE `sequence` GENRE'S guide/showcase.md FIGURE, chosen the way # `tcp-state-machine.fd` was chosen for the state figures: one real, # well-known protocol exchange that exercises essentially every # construct the genre has, so a reader sees the whole genre at work on # one page. All five keywords appear (`lifeline` `message` `state` # `fragment` `operand`), four of the twelve operators (`loop` `par` # `alt` `opt`), all three message operators, `in=` on ALL FIVE of its # acceptors — message, operand, lifeline, state and fragment — a state # INSIDE a fragment, and one level of fragment nesting — twice. # # WHY THIS FIGURE IS A `sequence` AND NOT A `statechart`. The corpus # already holds examples/statechart/dhcp-client.fd — the SAME protocol, # and correctly a statechart, because its subject is one machine's # modes and the lines between them are TRANSITIONS. This figure's # subject is three participants exchanging messages in time, and the # lines between them are MESSAGES. The many lines running between this # client and one server are the same pair exchanging DISCOVER / OFFER / # REQUEST / ACK / REQUEST / ACK / RELEASE over time, so a scene genre # would fan seven edges into one span; the statechart's many lines back # to INIT are DIFFERENT transitions of one machine and stay where they # are. It is not a `topology` either: `topology` reads a repeated node # pair as parallel LINKS, so a reading agent would answer "seven links # join the client and the server", which is wrong and carries nothing # to warn the reader. # # THE SOURCE FIGURE, AND WHERE THIS ONE GOES FURTHER. RFC 2131 # Figure 3's three columns are, left to right, "Server (not selected)", # "Client", "Server (selected)" — the first three lifelines below are # that order, because under this genre declaration order IS column # order. Figure 3 draws the acquisition only; §4.4.5's reacquisition # and §4.4.1's address check are prose in the RFC, and are drawn here. # The fourth lifeline is not in Figure 3 at all and is declared last so # that the RFC's own three columns keep their order. # # DIRECTION IS WRITTEN FROM THE CLIENT'S SIDE, consistently: what the # client SENDS is `message c -> …` and what it RECEIVES is # `message c <- …`. Both spellings draw the same arrow the same way; # writing them consistently is what makes the ladder scannable.
# ── HONEST LIMIT — a message is ONE instant ───────────────────────── # Every message below is one row: it has no send event and no separate # receive event, so the figure cannot say that a DHCPDISCOVER left the # client before the DHCPOFFER that answers it was even formed, and it # cannot draw propagation delay, overtaking, or a message still in # flight when the next one leaves. UML gives a Message two occurrence # specifications and draws the arrow sloped when the gap matters; this # genre draws one horizontal row per message. Nothing in this protocol # needed the distinction — but a figure about a slow link, or about two # messages crossing on the wire, could not be drawn here at all. # # ── HONEST LIMIT — no GeneralOrdering, so `par` is all-or-nothing ──── # Order in this genre is TOTAL: source order is time order. The one # escape is `type=par`, and it unorders EVERY pair inside it. UML's # escape from that is a GeneralOrdering — a constraint that re-orders # one chosen pair inside an otherwise unordered region — and this genre # deliberately does not spell it. The `offers` fragment below is where # it would be wanted: the two DHCPOFFERs genuinely have no relative # order, but if a figure wanted to say "A's offer may arrive before or # after B's, EXCEPT that both arrive before the DHCPREQUEST", the # second half of that sentence has no spelling. Here the containing # order gives it, so nothing is lost in THIS figure; a figure with two # interleaved concurrent exchanges would lose it. # # ── LIMIT LIFTED, and what is still true ───────────── # This block used to read: "a lifeline's state occurrences are read as # one sequence in document order, so a second INIT reads as restating a # state that has not changed and is refused as such … the DHCPDECLINE # restart travels in that message's `description=` and the DHCPNAK # restart is drawn." That was accurate about the engine and wrong about # the figure. RFC 2131 Figure 5 sends REQUESTING back to INIT on # DHCPNAK (§4.4.5) and §3.1 item 5 restarts from INIT after a # DHCPDECLINE, and the two paths are mutually exclusive in TIME — the # address either checks out or it does not — so neither INIT restates # the other. The check is OPERAND-SCOPED now: occurrences in different # operands of one fragment do not restate each other, and an occurrence # is compared only with the most recent one in a scope that encloses # its own. Both restarts are therefore drawn as states, and neither # fact rides in a `description=` any more. # WHAT IS STILL TRUE, and a reader must carry it: the state drawn AFTER # a fragment follows whichever operand ran, and the picture cannot mark # which. That is the same shape one step further on, and it is why the # final `state c "INIT"` below is compared with `REQUESTING` rather than # with anything inside the alternatives. # # ── HONEST LIMIT — a meaning-only class puts no ink on the page ──── # `class dropped "Sent, never delivered"` declares no paint, so the # legend prints the MEANING and no swatch, and the message that joins # it is drawn exactly like a message that arrived. The fact is in the # source, in the legend and in that message's `description=`; what the # PICTURE alone cannot say is WHICH message it was. A reader of the # `.fd` gets it, a reader of the `.svg` gets the sentence without its # subject. That is the price of carrying the fact in a class, and it is # stated here rather than left for a reader to notice. # # ── HONEST LIMIT — fan-out: one broadcast, drawn as N messages ────── # DHCPDISCOVER and the broadcast DHCPREQUEST are ONE datagram that # every server on the subnet receives, and Figure 3 draws that with a # single fanning glyph. FigDown has no fan-out construct, so each # broadcast is written as one message per recipient, and the `bcast` # class is what tells a reader they are one datagram. Mermaid cannot # draw it either, so it is a real-figure gap and not a coverage gap. # # ── HONEST LIMIT — Figure 3's floating captions are not drawn ─────── # Figure 3 writes "Determines configuration", "Collects replies", # "Selects configuration" and "Commits configuration" as captions # floating on a lifeline with NO arrow. There is no spelling for an # event with no arrow, and a self-message would draw an arrow the RFC # does not draw. They survive as `description=` prose on the # neighbouring messages. # # ── HONEST LIMIT — causal attribution ─────────────────────────────── # The figure asserts that the client's state changed at a POINT in the # exchange; it does not assert that the change was CAUSED by the # message before it. That needs an annotation key aimed at a message, # and a message has no id to aim at. # # ── HONEST LIMIT — `in=` on the fourth lifeline is model-only ─────── # `lifeline h … in=conflict` says that participant exists only inside # the address-conflict fragment, and the model records it. The drawing # does not shorten the column: h's dashed lifeline runs the full height # of the figure like every other. A reader who wants that fact reads it # from the source, which is the half of "one source, two readers" this # figure can still keep.
# ── Semantic classes — the meaning behind every stroke ────────────── # A reading agent queries these to group messages by role; the colour # is only presentation, the meaning is the label. Every stroke in this # figure carries a keyed meaning. class bcast "Broadcast to 255.255.255.255 — ONE datagram that every DHCP server on the subnet receives; drawn once per recipient because FigDown has no fan-out (RFC 2131 §4.1)" stroke=#2563eb class offer "Server's unsolicited offer of configuration parameters; the server need not reserve the address it offers (RFC 2131 §3.1 item 2)" stroke=#0891b2 class commit "Server commits the binding to persistent storage and confirms it (RFC 2131 §3.1 item 4)" stroke=#16a34a class refuse "Refusal or conflict — the client's notion of its address is wrong, or the address is already in use (RFC 2131 §3.1 items 4-5)" stroke=#dc2626 style=dashed class unicast "Addressed to one server only, using the address the client already holds (RFC 2131 §4.4.4)" stroke=#9333ea class probe "The client's own check on the link before it trusts the address (RFC 2131 §4.4.1)" stroke=#b45309 style=dashed # The meaning-only class: it declares NO paint at all, so it adds no # swatch and cannot collide with any other entry — it puts its MEANING # in the legend and nothing else. This is the idiom for a message that # was sent and never delivered: the class carries the fact, and the # per-message reason goes in `description=`. The message below joins it # alongside `unicast`, so the stroke says how it was addressed and this # says what became of it. class dropped "Sent, never delivered"
# ── The participants — RFC 2131 Figure 3's own column order ───────── # "not selected" / "selected" are Figure 3's own captions and describe # the ACQUISITION only: under §4.4.5 REBINDING, ANY server may extend # the lease, and below it is server A that does. lifeline sa "DHCP server A\n(not selected)" lifeline c "DHCP client" lifeline sb "DHCP server B\n(selected)" # Not in Figure 3: the host that already holds 192.0.2.44, which is why # the address check of §4.4.1 finds a conflict at all. It takes part in # nothing outside that check, and `in=` says so. lifeline h "Host already\nusing the address" in=conflict
# ═══ Acquisition — RFC 2131 §3.1, drawn as Figure 3 ═════════════════
# §4.4.1: "The client begins in INIT state and forms a DHCPDISCOVER # message." Figure 5 names the state. state c "INIT"
# §3.1 item 1 + §3.1 item 3: "The client times out and retransmits the # DHCPDISCOVER message if the client receives no DHCPOFFER messages", # under the randomized exponential backoff of §4.1 (4s, 8s, … 64s). fragment discover "until a DHCPOFFER arrives — randomized exponential backoff, §4.1" type=loop message c -> sa "DHCPDISCOVER xid=0x3d1f" in=discover class=bcast message c -> sb "DHCPDISCOVER xid=0x3d1f" in=discover class=bcast description="ciaddr=0, chaddr = the client's hardware address; the client waits 1-10s before the first send to desynchronize startup (§4.4.1)" # THE STATE SITS INSIDE THE LOOP, which is where §4.4.1 puts it: # Figure 5's arc out of INIT is labelled "/Send DHCPDISCOVER", so the # client is already in SELECTING for every retransmission after the # first. Drawn here, the box says the retransmissions happen in # SELECTING and not in INIT. state c "SELECTING" in=discover
# §3.1 item 2: "Each server may respond with a DHCPOFFER message." The # two replies have no relative order, which is what `par` says and the # total order otherwise forbids. Figure 3's "Determines configuration" # caption sits here on both server lifelines. fragment offers "each server may respond; the two replies have no relative order, §3.1 item 2" type=par operand oa "server A" in=offers message c <- sa "DHCPOFFER yiaddr=192.0.2.10" in=oa class=offer operand ob "server B" in=offers message c <- sb "DHCPOFFER yiaddr=192.0.2.44" in=ob class=offer description="lease=3600s, T1=1800s, T2=3150s; the server SHOULD check the address is not already in use, e.g. by an ICMP Echo Request (§3.1 item 2)"
# §3.1 item 3: the client collects the offers, selects one, and # BROADCASTS the DHCPREQUEST — so the server it did not select also # receives it and reads it as a declined offer (§3.1 item 4). message c -> sa "DHCPREQUEST server-id=B" class=bcast description="server A reads this as a declined offer and may return 192.0.2.10 to the pool (§3.1 item 4)" message c -> sb "DHCPREQUEST server-id=B" class=bcast description="requested-ip=192.0.2.44, and the same 'secs' value and broadcast address as the DHCPDISCOVER, so every relay agent forwards it to the same servers (§3.1 item 3)" state c "REQUESTING"
# §3.1 item 4: the selected server either commits the binding and # answers DHCPACK, or "SHOULD respond with a DHCPNAK message" if it # cannot satisfy the request. fragment commit "can the selected server still satisfy the request? §3.1 item 4" type=alt operand granted "yes — the server commits the binding" in=commit message c <- sb "DHCPACK yiaddr=192.0.2.44" in=granted class=commit description="the server commits the binding to persistent storage; 'yiaddr' carries the selected address and the lease options carry T1 and T2 (§3.1 item 4)" # THE STATE SITS INSIDE THE BRANCH THAT EARNED IT. §4.4.1: "Once the # DHCPACK message from the server arrives, the client is initialized # and moves to BOUND state." Only this operand reaches BOUND, and the # operand box is what says so. state c "BOUND" in=granted
# §3.1 item 5 / §4.4.1: "The client SHOULD perform a final check on the # parameters (e.g., ARP for allocated network address)." This is the # nested fragment — one level, which is the whole of this genre's # containment — and the only genuinely OPTIONAL part of the exchange. fragment conflict "only if the address turns out to be in use, §3.1 item 5" type=opt in=granted # `<->` is ONE occurrence, not two: an exchange in both directions # whose individual messages are not enumerated. That is exactly what # this is — an ARP request broadcast with sender-ip 0.0.0.0 (so other # ARP caches are not confused) and the ARP reply that comes back from # whoever holds the address. Both are messages of another protocol, and # RFC 2131 does not enumerate them; it says only that the check is # performed and what the client does when it fails. message c <-> h "ARP: who-has 192.0.2.44 — and the reply" in=conflict class=probe description="the client broadcasts with sender-ip 0.0.0.0; a reply means the address is already in use (§4.4.1)" # §3.1 item 5: the client "MUST send a DHCPDECLINE message to the # server and restarts the configuration process", waiting at least ten # seconds first. message c -> sb "DHCPDECLINE requested-ip=192.0.2.44" in=conflict class=refuse description="the client waits at least ten seconds before restarting (§3.1 item 5)" # AND THE RESTART IS NOW DRAWN. Until this release this INIT could only # travel in the message's description=: the no-restatement check read a # lifeline's occurrences as one linear sequence, so this INIT and the # DHCPNAK branch's INIT read as one restating the other. They are on # exclusive paths — the address either checks out or it does not, and the # server either commits or NAKs — and the check is operand-scoped now, so # both restarts are on the drawing where a reader can see them. state c "INIT" in=conflict
operand refused "no — the address is not available" in=commit message c <- sb "DHCPNAK" in=refused class=refuse description="the selected server cannot satisfy the request; Figure 5 sends REQUESTING back to INIT on DHCPNAK (§4.4.5)" state c "INIT" in=refused
# ═══ Reacquisition — RFC 2131 §4.4.5 ════════════════════════════════
# §4.4.5 is a CYCLE, and it is drawn as one: every lease held long # enough runs T1 → T2 → reacquisition and then runs it again, with the # three state changes that are the whole point of the renewal half # INSIDE the box. The T1 and T2 firings are in the message labels # themselves, because vertical distance in this genre carries no # duration and a reader has nowhere else to get the numbers. fragment renew "the reacquisition cycle — a renewed lease runs it again, §4.4.5" type=loop operand held "while the client holds the lease" in=renew # §4.4.5: "T1 is the time at which the client enters the RENEWING state # and attempts to contact the server that originally issued the # client's network address." state c "RENEWING" in=held # The DHCPREQUEST is unicast to the server that issued the lease and # MUST NOT carry a 'server identifier' option (§4.4.5). It joins two # classes: `unicast` for how it was addressed, `dropped` for what # became of it — the meaning-only class that says it was sent and never # delivered, with the per-message reason here in `description=`. message c -> sb "DHCPREQUEST ciaddr=192.0.2.44 — unicast at T1, 0.5 x the lease (1800s)" in=held class=unicast,dropped description="server B is unreachable; no DHCPACK arrives, which is what makes T2 fire (§4.4.5)"
# §4.4.5: "If no DHCPACK arrives before time T2, the client moves to # REBINDING state and sends (via broadcast) a DHCPREQUEST message to # extend its lease." The second nesting, one level inside the loop's # operand: the whole T2 half happens only when T1 went unanswered. fragment rebind "only if no DHCPACK arrived before T2 — 0.875 x the lease (3150s), §4.4.5" type=opt in=held state c "REBINDING" in=rebind message c -> sa "DHCPREQUEST ciaddr=192.0.2.44 — broadcast at T2" in=rebind class=bcast message c -> sb "DHCPREQUEST ciaddr=192.0.2.44 — broadcast at T2" in=rebind class=bcast description="broadcast so that ANY server may extend the lease; this is why server A, which was not selected in §3.1, can answer it" # §4.4.5: "The client has successfully reacquired its network address, # returns to BOUND state and may continue network processing." message c <- sa "DHCPACK lease=3600s" in=rebind class=commit description="the binding server is now A (§4.4.5)" state c "BOUND" in=rebind
# ═══ Release — RFC 2131 §3.1 item 6 and §4.4.6 ══════════════════════
# Figure 3's "Graceful shutdown" caption sits here. §4.4.6 notes that # "the correct operation of DHCP does not depend on the transmission of # DHCPRELEASE messages", which is why this is the last thing drawn and # not a required one. message c -> sa "DHCPRELEASE ciaddr=192.0.2.44" class=unicast description="Figure 3 captions the server side 'Discards lease'" state c "INIT"
